assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new observational window is what I value most: the detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos in a cubic-kilometre Antarctic ice detector turned a decades-old instrument dream into neutrino astronomy. The original idea, the engineering of optical modules in deep ice and the calibration of ice properties were hard, patient detector work, and the physics (cosmic-ray origins, a first source association, Galactic-plane neutrinos) is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Halzen drove the concept and the collaboration for decades and Karle was central to the detector construction and the discovery analyses. The credited pair is a fair, compact configuration, though a collaboration of several hundred and other pioneers (e.g. earlier DUMAND and AMANDA groups) make the allocation of credit a real question.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation is good: the diffuse flux is established at high significance through several analysis channels, with TXS 0506+056 evidence and the Galactic-plane result adding source-level support. Neutrino astronomy is young but the core discovery is stable, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the credited pair adequately represents a large collaboration and its predecessors.
Source-level associations (e.g. TXS 0506+056) rest on lower significance than the diffuse flux.
I rely on my general knowledge of IceCube's history and have not verified specific credit details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea and its realisation at unprecedented stability and accuracy, is a major leap in measurement science. It underpins redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. It is an instrument-driven advance of exactly the kind that rewards years of control of systematics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and built the first strontium lattice clock; Ye brought the clock to record accuracy and stability and pushed the many-body and relativistic applications. The two-person credit is clean and defensible.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs reproduce and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, so confirmation is excellent. Impact is well established and the field is mature, though a redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
uncertainties: Neighbouring contributors in ion clocks and frequency combs have been recognised already or could claim overlap.
AMO precision measurement is outside my own expertise, so I would lean on colleagues for the credit boundaries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson required two general-purpose detectors, trigger and data-handling systems of unprecedented scale and a decades-long programme of calibration and systematic control. The 2013 prize recognised the theory; the measurement and the instruments that delivered it have a strong claim to their own recognition and have defined modern particle physics.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over thousands of people. Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, as founding or leading figures of ATLAS and CMS, give a defensible three-person set, but this choice leaves out Virdee and other design leaders, and any pick is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Two independent experiments confirmed the particle and coupling measurements have matured over a decade, so the result is secure. The prize is arguably overdue rather than premature, though the 2013 award reduces urgency.
uncertainties: Rules limit the prize to three people, so the allocation among many leaders is inherently arbitrary and may be seen as unfair.
The 2013 prize partly covered the same discovery, which may reduce the appetite for a second award.
I have not verified the exact roles of each credited person.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 founded quantum cryptography, a concrete route from basic quantum principles to secure communication. The importance and originality are high, and the field has produced real satellite and fibre demonstrations. This sits in quantum information, where I would defer to colleagues on depth.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84 and are the natural core. Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is independent in conception and a legitimate claim; with only three places the choice between him and the BB84 pair is not trivial, and I take the BB84 pair as the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: BB84 has been implemented in many independent experiments and commercial systems. The theoretical security proofs and practical side-channel issues are still being worked on, but the concept is stable and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether Ekert should be included or whether the prize should cover teleportation-related work (see the similar candidate B016).
Practical security of real devices is not fully settled.
Outside my core expertise, so I rely on colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip, drift and hybrid pixel detectors made precision vertexing and tracking possible at modern colliders and have spread to astrophysics and medical imaging. As an instrument builder I regard detector inventions of this kind as underrated; Charpak's 1992 prize shows precedent. The impact on charm and beauty physics, the Higgs and space instruments is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer's planar process and silicon detectors, Parker's microstrip devices and Heijne's pixel work are the usual core, but many others (e.g. Rancoita, Hall, Campbell and the CERN pixel groups) share the field. Credit allocation is the main weakness.
assessment.maturity: The technology is mature, universally adopted and independently validated over four decades, so there is no doubt about maturity. Timeliness is a mild concern because the key inventions are old and some inventors have died.
uncertainties: Whether all decisive inventors are alive and whether the three credited names capture the decisive contributions.
The credited names may mix distinct inventions (microstrip, drift and pixel) that could need different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Imaging the shadows of M87* and Sgr A* with an Earth-sized interferometer is a landmark measurement that opened direct study of strong-field gravity at the horizon. The instrument and calibration challenge, including VLBI at 1.3 mm, is the kind of patient work I respect.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow concept for imaging and Doeleman led the VLBI development and the collaboration. Zensus is a leading instrument and institutional figure. A fair prize with three names is possible, but the work belongs to a collaboration of hundreds.
assessment.maturity: The images have been reproduced across epochs and data sets, and Sgr A* followed. Interpretation and parameter estimates (spin, accretion model) remain model-dependent, so the maturity is good for imaging but partial for the physics.
uncertainties: Credit for a very large collaboration is difficult to compress into one to three people.
Model-dependent interpretation of the images.
Whether the prize would be seen as overlapping with the 2020 black-hole prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at magic angles and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened a new field of moire materials with a rich tunable phase diagram. Originality and influence are very high.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive experimental discoveries. A theory plus experiment pairing is natural, though the choice between MacDonald and Bistritzer and the role of other experimental groups is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce the phases, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated, so some would call the recognition early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled.
Allocation among theory contributors.
Condensed matter is outside my expertise and I defer to colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal of how to realise quantum gates with cold trapped ions and later quantum simulation with cold atoms was a foundational idea that guided experiments across several platforms. The impact on quantum information science is strong and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are jointly credited with the original ion-trap gate proposal, a clean two-person theoretical credit. Experimental realisations by Wineland and Blatt groups are separately credited elsewhere in the list.
assessment.maturity: The proposal has been confirmed in numerous experiments and is an enabling concept for current ion-trap quantum computers, so maturity is high. Recognition of experimentalists in 2012 reduces some pressure on a theory prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with candidates B007 and B032 that share Zoller.
Outside my core expertise, so I rely on colleagues for the weighting.
